full_judgment:
2. The petitioner who is a young lady, at present a student of the Dhaka University in the Department of English, has moved this writ petition on the allegations, inter alia, that she was legally married to respondents No. 1 namely Major Sabbir Ahmed now a student officer at Defence Command & Staff College at Mirpur Cantonment, Mirpur, on 18.12.86 when she was only 19 years of age. It is the case of the petitioner that after her marriage she mostly stayed with her parents while respondent being in defence service was transferred to various parts of the country and thus the petitioner No. 2 never had a marital home of their own with the respondent though petitioner No. 2 at various times lived with respondent in the quarter allotted by the Government as a visitor. On 24.8.88 a child was born of the said wedlock and the child since then had been living with his mother and both had been living in the maternal grand father's home all along. The marriage was not a happy one. According to the petitioner wife, there was incompatibility of temperament and it is alleged by the petitioner that the husband often misbehaved with her. The petitioner tried to reason with him and tried to build a home but in vain. Her husband, according to the petitioner, had been cruel and did not take care. The child was named as 'Awad Sameh Sabbir' and had been studying in the English medium school at Sun Beam School since January 1992. The petitioner having come to the conclusion that there is no way out but to separate decided to divorce her husband which she did by way of an affidavit on 25.11.92 and she sent a copy of the said to the Chairman of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation as required under section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance.. The notice along with a copy of the affidavit has also been sent to the husband which he has received on 30.11.92. According to the petitioner, after the divorce notice the father of the child became violent and started threatening her, complaining about the notice of divorce, asking her to withdraw it and also threatening that her son will be abducted. The petitioner had been regularly taking her child to the school and also used to bring him back after the school hour. On 13.12.92 she went to collect her child at about 11:15 A.M from the school but found that the child was being dragged to a baby taxi by the respondent who having put the child in a baby taxi tried to run away. The petitioner objected to the same and she raised hue and cry but to no result. The child was taken by the scooter driver along with respondent husband. The petitioner No. 2 thereafter tried to contact the respondent but she failed. The petitioner also tried to contact the members of her in-laws families but to no result. Instead, she received telephone calls with threatening words, through the friends of the respondent. The petitioner was also told that she ought to remember that respondent works in the defence service and it would not be easy to get anything from him. The petitioner then approached the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad for protecting her child and the Mahila Parishad is petitioner No. 1 along with this petitioner before this court. She served a demand justice notice through her lawyer asking to return the child but no result, hence this application under Article 102(2)(b)(i) of the Constitution in the nature of a Habeas Corpus petition. 

 7. The learned Advocate for the respondent husband submits that this is not a case of kidnapping but an act done perhaps in misunderstanding of the law but not wilfully. According to the learned Advocate, this court may pass the order as the court may think fit and proper giving custody of the child to the mother but with a direction that the father would have some access to the son, even meet him at a neutral place without interference, when the custody of the son will be with the mother. 

 8. Before coming to the factual aspect of the matter and the rival contentions, we would like to mention that the provision of Article 102(2)(b) of the Constitution is very wide in nature as it provided that any person and not only aggrieved person as in mandamus or certiorari or quo warranto can take to the notice of the court that somebody is illegally detained by any person and pray for a declaration that the person is so detained illegally and without lawful authority and the court shall, after being so satisfied, direct the person to be set at liberty at once. But this is a writ against executive order. Would it be extended to a private detention committed after abduction by an individual. The answer is in the affirmative. 

 9. A petition in this nature of habeas corpus for the custody of a minor would also be equally competent without sending the petitioner to exhaust his or her remedy before the Family Court or under the Guardians and Wards Act or other criminal Court which is neither expedient nor an equally efficacious remedy in a situation like this and, in fact, a habeas corpus petition would give her the most speeedy and efficacious remedy. 

 10. In the case of Goher Begum Vs. Suggi, reported in AIR 1960 (SC) 93 a similar question of maintainability of a petition in Habeas Corpus under section 491 CrPC to restore a minor child from father when there are remedies under the provisions of the Guardians and Wards Act, was considered, and it was held that there is no reason why the appellant should not proceed under the Guardians and Wards Act for recovery of the custody of the child. It was further held that she has a right to go under the Guardians and Wards Act and also in Habeas Corpus under section 491 CrPC. 

 12. We having also considered that this writ is maintainable, and having never wished to relegate her to the long drawn process of a litigation, decided to proceed with the matter early and directed the minor to be produced before this court on the date fixed and after having viewed the father, the mother and the minor boy we had been happy to see that the boy, who is nearly 3½ years of age, is attached to both the mother and the father and he occasionally changed laps from mother to the father and father to the mother, and had been constantly talking, to himself of course, which voice of such a child is rarely heard in this court room and keeping in mind the fact that the father and the mother is in the process of being separated being divorced by the mother, the minor boy cannot live both with the mother and the father at the same time as would be the case with millions of children in the country, but not with him. He should be delivered to the person who is entitled to his custody. 

 13. While dealing with matters referable to the custody of a child, the established legal position is that the welfare of the child is of prime consideration. The provisions of the personal law of the parties or even the provisions of the statute law as to such custody may be subject to that paramount need of the welfare of the child has also held in the case of Smt. Surinder Kaur Sandhu reported in AIR 1984 (SC) 1224 wherein the Supreme Court of India held thus: 

 14. Hence the court is to consider not only whether a boy or a girl has been detained in an unlawful or illegal manner but also whether he or she has been so kept to the prejudice of the person who, under the personal law of the parties and in view of the welfare of the child, is entitled to the custody even if it comes into conflict with our statute law. 

 15. This brings us to personal law of the parties, namely the principles of Mohammadan Law. Under section 352 of the Mullah's Mohammadan Law the mother is the natural guardian till the child is seven years of age if male, and if female till she reached the age of puberty. In the instant case there is no dispute that the child is below seven years of age and is admitted to be a child of four years. The minor boy has been produced before this Court by the respondent in compliance to the order of this court. We have looked at the boy and to us he appears to be about 4 years of age, intelligent and capable of understanding affection. Thus, under the personal law of the party, admittedly belonging to Hanafi School, the custody of the child would be with the mother and she is thus, entitled to that custody immediately and also so entitled to that custody keeping in mind the welfare of the child. The personal law and the welfare doctrine are not in conflict here as to custody and even if they were, the welfare doctrine would have precedence. 

 17. We therefore, in open court direct the son, who is present in court, to be handed over to the custody of the mother and he is so handed over in presence of the parties. From now on, the mother would have the custody of the said minor son till he is seven years of age. This order has been passed by the court keeping open any further action for reconciliation that may be done. It should be kept in mind by the petitioner mother that if she remarries the question of custody of the child would be reviewed and the law will taka its course. 

 18. The contention of the learned Advocate Abdul Momen Choudhury has substance to the extent that in spite of the son being handed over to the custody of the mother, the father would have some access to the child. We also feel that way. In Imtiaz Banu's case, as narrated earlier, the Allahabad High Court also passed a similar order allowing access to the father.
